paragraphs: This first natural cause of inferiority is joined by another that comes from the laws. We have already seen that slavery, which has been abolished in the North, still exists in the South, and I have pointed out its fatal consequences for the prosperity of the planter himself.

The North is therefore superior to the South in both commerce *m and manufacturing, and the natural result is a more rapid growth of population and wealth within its borders. The States on the shores of the Atlantic Ocean are already half-peopled. Most of the land there has an owner, so these districts cannot take in as many emigrants as the Western States, where a boundless field is still open to their efforts. The valley of the Mississippi is far more fertile than the Atlantic coast. This reason, added to all the others, drives Europeans westward — a fact that can be demonstrated rigorously with figures. The total population of all the United States has roughly tripled over forty years. But in the new States next to the Mississippi, the population has grown thirty-one-fold in the same period. *n
m [ The following figures will be enough to show the difference between the commerce of the South and that of the North: —

In 1829 the combined tonnage of all the merchant vessels belonging to Virginia, the two Carolinas, and Georgia (the four great Southern States) came to only 5,243 tons. In the same year the tonnage of the vessels of the State of Massachusetts alone came to 17,322 tons. (See Legislative Documents, 21st Congress, 2d session, No. 140, p. 244.) So Massachusetts had three times as much shipping as the four States just named. Yet the area of Massachusetts is only 7,335 square miles, and its population is 610,014 inhabitants [2,238,943 in 1890], while the area of the four other States I have cited is 210,000 square miles and their population 3,047,767. Thus the area of Massachusetts is only one-thirtieth of the area of the four States, and its population is five times smaller than theirs. (See “Darby’s View of the United States.”) Slavery harms the commercial prosperity of the South in several ways: it weakens the spirit of enterprise among the whites, and it prevents them from finding as large a class of sailors as they need. Sailors are usually drawn from the lowest ranks of the population. But in the Southern States these lowest ranks consist of slaves, and it is very difficult to employ them at sea. They cannot serve as well as a white crew, and there would always be fear that they would mutiny in mid-ocean or escape in the foreign countries where they might put in.]
n [ “Darby’s View of the United States,” p. 444.]

The position of the central federal power relative to the population is continually shifting. Forty years ago most of the citizens of the Union lived on the Atlantic coast, in the area around the spot where Washington now stands. But the great body of the people is now moving inland and to the north, so that within twenty years the majority will undoubtedly be on the western side of the Alleghanies. If the Union continues to exist, the basin of the Mississippi is clearly marked out, by its fertility and its size, as the future center of the Federal Government. In thirty or forty years that region will have taken the rank that naturally belongs to it. It is easy to calculate that its population, compared to that of the Atlantic coast, will be, in round numbers, as 40 to 11. In a few years the States that founded the Union will lose the direction of its policy, and the population of the valley of the Mississippi will predominate in the federal assemblies.

This constant shift of federal power and influence toward the northwest shows itself every ten years, when a general census is taken and the number of delegates each State sends to Congress is set anew. *o In 1790 Virginia had nineteen representatives in Congress. That number kept rising until 1813, when it reached twenty-three; from then on it declined, and in 1833 Virginia elected only twenty-one representatives. *p Over the same period the State of New York moved in the opposite direction: in 1790 it had ten representatives in Congress; in 1813, twenty-seven; in 1823, thirty-four; and in 1833, forty. The State of Ohio had only one representative in 1803, and in 1833 it already had nineteen.

o [ It can be seen that over the last ten years (1820-1830) the population of one district, for instance the State of Delaware, has grown by five percent, while that of another, such as the territory of Michigan, has grown by 250 percent. Likewise the population of Virginia had increased thirteen percent, and that of the border State of Ohio sixty-one percent, in the same period. The general table of these changes, given in the “National Calendar,” presents a striking picture of the unequal fortunes of the different States.]

p [ It was just said that in the last period the population of Virginia grew thirteen percent. It is necessary to explain how the number of representatives for a State can fall when the State’s population, far from shrinking, is actually growing. I take the State of Virginia, which I have already mentioned, as my point of comparison. The number of Virginia’s representatives in 1823 was proportional to the total number of representatives of the Union and to the ratio of its population to that of the whole Union. In 1833 the number of Virginia’s representatives was likewise proportional to the total number of representatives of the Union and to the ratio of its population, enlarged over ten years, to the enlarged population of the Union over the same time. The new number of Virginian representatives will then stand to the old number, on the one hand, as the new total number of representatives stands to the old; and, on the other hand, as the growth of Virginia’s population stands to the growth of the whole population of the country. Thus, if the growth of the smaller country’s population stands to that of the larger in exact inverse ratio to the proportion between the new and old totals of representatives, the number of Virginia’s representatives will stay the same. And if the growth of the Virginian population stands to that of the whole Union in a weaker ratio than the new number of the Union’s representatives to the old number, the number of Virginia’s representatives must fall. [Thus, to the 56th Congress in 1899, Virginia and West Virginia send only fourteen representatives.]]

It is hard to imagine a lasting union between a rich, strong people and a poor, weak one, even if it were proved that the strength and wealth of the one are not the causes of the weakness and poverty of the other. But union is harder still to maintain when one party is losing strength and the other is gaining it. This rapid and disproportionate growth of certain States threatens the independence of the others. New York, with its 2,000,000 inhabitants and its forty representatives, might perhaps succeed in dictating to the other States in Congress. But even if the more powerful States make no attempt to overbear the lesser ones, the danger remains, for the possibility of the act is almost as much to the point as the act itself. The weak generally distrust the justice and the reasonableness of the strong. The States that grow less rapidly than the others look with envy and suspicion on those that fortune favors more. Hence come the deep-seated uneasiness and vague agitation that can be observed in the South, and that contrast so sharply with the confidence and prosperity common to other parts of the Union. I am inclined to think that the hostile measures taken by the Southern provinces on a recent occasion are due to no other cause. Of all Americans, the inhabitants of the Southern States have the greatest interest in maintaining the Union; they would surely suffer most from being left to themselves; and yet they are the only citizens who threaten to break the bond of confederation. But it is easy to see that the South has given the Union four Presidents, Washington, Jefferson, Madison, and Monroe; that it perceives it is losing its federal influence; and that the number of its representatives in Congress is shrinking from year to year, while those of the Northern and Western States are growing. The South is peopled with ardent and irascible men, and it is becoming more and more irritated and alarmed. Its citizens reflect on their present position and remember their past influence, with the melancholy uneasiness of men who suspect oppression. If they find a law of the Union that is not unequivocally favorable to their interests, they protest against it as an abuse of force; and if their ardent remonstrances go unheard, they threaten to leave an association that loads them with burdens while it deprives them of their due profits. “The tariff,” said the inhabitants of Carolina in 1832, “enriches the North, and ruins the South; for if this were not the case, to what can we attribute the continually increasing power and wealth of the North, with its inclement skies and arid soil; while the South, which may be styled the garden of America, is rapidly declining?” *q
q [ See the report of its committee to the Convention which proclaimed the nullification of the tariff in South Carolina.]

If the changes I have described were gradual, so that each generation at least had time to pass away along with the order of things it had lived under, the danger would be smaller. But the progress of society in America is precipitate and almost revolutionary. The same citizen may live to see his State take the lead in the Union and then become powerless in the federal assemblies; and an Anglo-American republic has been known to grow as fast as a man passing from birth and infancy to maturity in thirty years. It must not be imagined, however, that States that lose their predominance also lose their population or their wealth. Their prosperity is not halted, and they even go on growing faster than any kingdom in Europe. *r But they believe themselves impoverished because their wealth does not grow as fast as their neighbors’, and they think their power is lost because they have suddenly run up against a power greater than their own. *s Thus they are hurt more in their feelings and passions than in their interests. But that is amply enough to endanger the maintenance of the Union. If kings and peoples had only ever looked to their true interests since the beginning of the world, the name of war would scarcely be known among mankind.

r [ The population of a country is surely the first element of its wealth. In the ten years (1820-1830) during which Virginia lost two of its representatives in Congress, its population grew by 13.7 percent, that of Carolina by fifteen percent, and that of Georgia by 15.5 percent. (See the “American Almanac,” 1832, p. 162) But the population of Russia, which grows faster than that of any other European country, increases in ten years at only 9.5 percent; in France, at seven percent; and in Europe in general, at 4.7 percent. (See “Malte Brun,” vol. vi. p. 95)]

s [ It must be admitted, however, that the fall in the value of tobacco over the last fifty years has notably reduced the opulence of the Southern planters; but this circumstance is as independent of the will of their Northern brethren as it is of their own.]

So the prosperity of the United States is the source of the gravest dangers that threaten them. It tends to produce, in some of the confederate States, the feverish excitement that comes with fast-growing fortunes, and to awaken in others the envy, mistrust, and regret that usually follow when such fortunes are lost. The Americans watch this extraordinary and hurried progress with exultation, but they would be wiser to watch it with sorrow and alarm. The Americans of the United States are bound to become one of the greatest nations in the world. Their offshoot will cover almost all of North America, and the continent they live on is their dominion, which cannot slip away from them. What drives them to seize it so soon? Riches, power, and renown will certainly be theirs someday, yet they rush toward their fortune as though only a moment were left to make it their own.

I think I have shown that the existence of the present confederation depends entirely on the continued assent of all the confederates, and, starting from this principle, I have inquired into the causes that may lead the several States to separate from the others. The Union may, however, perish in two different ways. One of the confederate States may choose to withdraw from the compact and so forcibly sever the federal tie; most of my remarks so far apply to this supposition. Or the authority of the Federal Government may be gradually eroded by the simultaneous tendency of the united republics to take back their independence. The central power, stripped one by one of all its prerogatives and reduced to impotence by tacit consent, would become unable to fulfill its purpose, and the second Union would perish, like the first, from a kind of senile incapacity. The gradual weakening of the federal tie, which may finally lead to the dissolution of the Union, is a separate matter, and it may produce a variety of lesser consequences before it brings about so violent a change. The confederation might still subsist even if its government were reduced to such a state of inanition that it paralyzed the nation, caused internal anarchy, and checked the general prosperity of the country.

Having investigated the causes that may lead the Anglo-Americans to disunite, it is important to ask whether, if the Union continues to exist, their government will widen or narrow its sphere of action, and whether it will become more energetic or weaker.

The Americans are evidently disposed to view their future condition with alarm. They see that in most nations of the world the exercise of the rights of sovereignty tends to fall under the control of a few individuals, and they are dismayed by the idea that the same will happen in their own country. Even statesmen feel these fears, or pretend to; for in America centralization is by no means popular, and there is no surer way of courting the majority than to inveigh against the encroachments of the central power. The Americans do not notice that the countries where this alarming tendency to centralization exists are inhabited by a single people, while the fact that the Union is composed of different confederate communities is enough to defeat all the inferences that might be drawn from analogous circumstances. I confess that I am inclined to consider the fears of a great number of Americans as purely imaginary; and far from sharing their dread of power being consolidated in the hands of the Union, I think that the Federal Government is visibly losing strength.
To prove this assertion I shall not turn to any remote events, but to circumstances that I have witnessed myself and that belong to our own time.

A careful look at what is going on in the United States will easily convince us that two opposite tendencies exist in that country, like two distinct currents flowing in opposite directions in the same channel. The Union has now existed for forty-five years, and in that time a vast number of provincial prejudices, which at first were hostile to its power, have died away. The patriotic feeling that attached each American to his native State has become less exclusive, and the different parts of the Union have become more closely connected the better they have come to know each other. The post, *t that great instrument of intellectual communication, now reaches into the backwoods, and steamboats have established daily connections between the different points of the coast. An inland navigation of unexampled speed carries goods up and down the rivers of the country. *u To these advantages of nature and art we may add those restless cravings, that busy-mindedness, and that love of money, which constantly drive the American into active life and bring him into contact with his fellow citizens. He crosses the country in every direction; he visits all the various populations of the land; and there is not a province in France whose natives know each other as well as the 13,000,000 men who cover the territory of the United States.

t [ In 1832 the district of Michigan, which has only 31,639 inhabitants and is still nearly unexplored wilderness, already had 940 miles of mail-roads. The territory of Arkansas, which is even less settled, was already crossed by 1,938 miles of mail-roads. (See the report of the General Post Office, November 30, 1833.) The postage on newspapers alone in the whole Union came to $254,796.]

u [ In the ten years from 1821 to 1831, 271 steamboats were launched on the rivers that water the valley of the Mississippi alone. In 1829, 259 steamboats existed in the United States. (See Legislative Documents, No. 140, p. 274.)]

But as the Americans intermingle, they come to resemble each other more. The differences that result from their climate, their origin, and their institutions grow smaller, and they all draw nearer and nearer to a common type. Every year, thousands of men leave the North to settle in different parts of the Union. They bring with them their faith, their opinions, and their customs; and as they are better educated than the men among whom they are about to live, they soon rise to the head of affairs and shape society to their own advantage. This continual emigration from the North to the South is particularly favorable to the fusion of all the different provincial characters into one national character. The civilization of the North appears to be the common standard to which the whole nation will one day be assimilated.

The commercial ties that unite the confederate States are strengthened by the Americans’ growing manufactures, and the union that began to exist in their opinions gradually becomes part of their habits. The passage of time has swept away the bugbear fears that haunted the imaginations of citizens in 1789. The federal power has not become oppressive; it has not destroyed the independence of the States; it has not subjected the confederates to monarchical institutions; and the Union has not made the lesser States dependent on the larger ones. Instead the confederation has gone on growing in population, wealth, and power. I am therefore convinced that the natural obstacles to the continuance of the American Union are not as powerful at present as they were in 1789, and that the enemies of the Union are not as numerous.

Nevertheless, a careful examination of the history of the United States over the last forty-five years will readily convince us that the federal power is declining, and it is not hard to explain the causes of this phenomenon. *v When the Constitution of 1789 was promulgated, the nation was a prey to anarchy. The Union that followed this confusion aroused much dread and much animosity, but it was warmly supported because it met a pressing need. So although it was more attacked then than it is now, the federal power soon reached the maximum of its authority, as usually happens with a government that triumphs after having braced its strength in the struggle. At that time the interpretation of the Constitution seemed to extend rather than restrain federal sovereignty, and in several respects the Union presented the appearance of a single, undivided people directed in its foreign and internal policy by a single government. But to reach this point the people had risen, to a certain extent, above itself.
v [ [Since 1861 the movement is certainly in the opposite direction, and the federal power has largely increased, and tends to further increase.]]

The Constitution had not destroyed the distinct sovereignty of the States, and all communities, of whatever kind, are driven by a secret propensity to assert their independence. This propensity is even stronger in a country like America, where every village forms a kind of republic accustomed to managing its own affairs. It therefore cost the States an effort to submit to federal supremacy, and all efforts, however successful, necessarily subside along with the causes that gave rise to them.

As the Federal Government consolidated its authority, America resumed its rank among the nations, peace returned to its frontiers, and public credit was restored. Confusion gave way to a settled state of things, which favored the full and free exercise of industrious enterprise. This very prosperity made the Americans forget the cause to which it was owed; and once the danger had passed, the energy and patriotism that had enabled them to face it disappeared from among them. No sooner were they freed from the cares that oppressed them than they easily returned to their ordinary habits and gave themselves up without resistance to their natural inclinations. When a powerful government no longer seemed necessary, they began once more to find it irksome. The Union encouraged general prosperity, and the States were not inclined to abandon the Union; but they wished to make the action of the power that represented it as light as possible. The general principle of Union was adopted, but in every minor detail there was an actual tendency toward independence. The principle of confederation was every day more easily admitted and more rarely applied; so the Federal Government brought about its own decline while it was creating order and peace.

As soon as this tendency of public opinion began to show itself outwardly, the leaders of parties, who live by the passions of the people, began to turn it to their own advantage. The position of the Federal Government then became extremely critical. Its enemies had won the popular favor, and they gained the right to direct its policy by pledging to reduce its influence. From that time forward the government of the Union has invariably been forced to give way whenever it has tried to enter the lists against the governments of the States. And whenever an interpretation of the terms of the Federal Constitution has been called for, that interpretation has most often gone against the Union and in favor of the States.

The Constitution gave the Federal Government the right to provide for the interests of the nation, and it had been held that no other authority was so well suited to superintend the “internal improvements” that affected the prosperity of the whole Union, such as the cutting of canals. But the States were alarmed at a power distinct from their own that could thus dispose of a portion of their territory. They were afraid that the central government would in this way acquire a formidable amount of patronage within their own borders and exercise a degree of influence that they intended to reserve exclusively for their own agents. The Democratic party, which has constantly opposed the growth of federal authority, then accused Congress of usurpation and the Chief Magistrate of ambition. The central government was intimidated by the opposition; it soon acknowledged its error, promising to confine its influence strictly in the future within the circle prescribed to it.

The Constitution gives the Union the right to treat with foreign nations. The Native American tribes on the frontiers of the United States had usually been regarded in this light. As long as these savages consented to retire before the civilized settlers, the federal right was not contested. But as soon as a tribe tried to settle in a fixed place, the adjacent States claimed possession of the lands and the rights of sovereignty over the natives. The central government soon recognized both claims; and after concluding treaties with the tribes as independent nations, it handed them over as subjects to the legislative tyranny of the States. *w

w [ See in the Legislative Documents, already cited where I spoke of the Native Americans, the letter of the President of the United States to the Cherokees, his correspondence on this subject with his agents, and his messages to Congress.]

Some of the States founded on the Atlantic coast extended indefinitely westward, into wild regions that no European had ever entered. The States whose boundaries were irrevocably fixed looked jealously at the unbounded regions that the future would let their neighbors explore. The latter then agreed, in order to conciliate the others and to make union easier, to set their own boundaries and to give up to the confederation at large all the territory beyond those limits. *x From then on the Federal Government became the owner of all the uncultivated lands lying beyond the borders of the thirteen States first confederated. It was given the right to divide and sell them, and the sums derived from this source were reserved exclusively for the public treasury of the Union, to provide funds for purchasing tracts of country from the Native Americans, for opening roads to the remote settlements, and for hastening the advance of civilization as much as possible. In the course of time, however, new States have been formed in the midst of the wilds formerly ceded by the inhabitants of the Atlantic shores. Congress has gone on selling, for the profit of the nation at large, the uncultivated lands these new States contained. But the new States at length asserted that, now that they were fully constituted, they ought to have the exclusive right to use the proceeds of these sales for themselves. As their remonstrances grew more and more threatening, Congress thought fit to deprive the Union of some of the privileges it had hitherto enjoyed; and at the end of 1832 it passed a law by which most of the revenue from the sale of lands was made over to the new western republics, although the lands themselves were not ceded to them. *y

x [ The first act of cession was made by the State of New York in 1780; Virginia, Massachusetts, Connecticut, and South and North Carolina followed this example at different times, and the act of cession of Georgia came as recently as 1802.]
y [ It is true that the President refused his assent to this law, but he fully adopted it in principle. (See Message of December 8, 1833.)]

Even a slight acquaintance with the United States lets one see what the country gains from the bank. The advantages are of several kinds, but one strikes a foreign visitor especially. Banknotes of the United States are accepted at the edge of the wilderness for the same value as in Philadelphia, where the bank carries on its business. *z

z [ The present Bank of the United States was established in 1816 with a capital of $35,000,000; its charter expires in 1836. Last year Congress passed a law to renew it, but the President vetoed the bill. The struggle is still going on with great violence on both sides, and the bank’s speedy fall may easily be foreseen. [It was soon afterwards extinguished by General Jackson.]]

Nevertheless, the Bank of the United States is the target of great animosity. Its directors have openly declared themselves enemies of the President, and they are accused, with some plausibility, of having misused their influence to block his election. The President therefore attacks the institution they represent with the heat of personal hatred, and he is spurred on in his revenge by the belief that the hidden leanings of the majority are on his side. The bank can be seen as the great monetary tie of the Union, just as Congress is the great legislative tie; and the same passions that tend to make the States independent of the central power also help to bring the bank down.

The Bank of the United States always holds a large number of notes issued by the provincial banks, and it can compel them at any time to redeem these in cash. It has nothing to fear from the same demand itself, because its resources are large enough to meet every claim. The provincial banks, however, are thereby threatened and their operations limited, since they may issue only as many notes as is proper for their capital. They put up with this healthy restraint impatiently. The newspapers they have bought, and the President, whose interest makes him their tool, attack the bank with the greatest violence. They stir up the local passions and the blind democratic instinct of the country on their side, and they claim that the bank directors form a permanent aristocratic body whose influence must eventually be felt in the government and must damage the principles of equality on which society in America rests.

The contest between the bank and its opponents is only an incident in the great struggle going on in America between the provinces and the central power, between the spirit of democratic independence and the spirit of gradation and subordination. I do not mean that the enemies of the bank are exactly the same individuals who attack the Federal Government on other points. But I assert that the attacks on the Bank of the United States spring from the same propensities that work against the Federal Government, and that the very numerous opponents of the bank are a deplorable symptom of the declining support for the government.

The Union has never shown such weakness as in the famous tariff question. *a The wars of the French Revolution and of 1812 had called manufacturing establishments into being in the North of the Union, because they cut off all free communication between America and Europe. When peace came and trade reopened, so that European goods again flowed to the New World, the Americans decided to set up a system of import duties with two aims: to protect their infant manufactures and to pay off the debt run up during the war. The Southern States, which have no manufactures to encourage and are purely agricultural, soon complained of this measure. Those were the plain facts, and I do not claim to examine here whether the complaints were well founded or unjust.
a [ For the details of this affair, see principally the Legislative Documents, 22d Congress, 2d Session, No. 30.]

As early as 1820, South Carolina declared in a petition to Congress that the tariff was “unconstitutional, oppressive, and unjust.” The States of Georgia, Virginia, North Carolina, Alabama, and Mississippi later protested against it with more or less vigor. But Congress, far from listening to these complaints, raised the scale of tariff duties in 1824 and 1828 and recognized anew the principle on which it was founded. A doctrine was then proclaimed in the South, or rather revived, which took the name of Nullification.

I showed in its proper place that the aim of the Federal Constitution was not to form a league but to create a national government. In every case that the Constitution specifies, the Americans of the United States are one undivided people, and on those points the will of the nation is expressed, as in all constitutional nations, through the voice of the majority. Once the majority has announced its decision, the minority has a duty to submit. That is the sound legal doctrine, and the only one consistent with the text of the Constitution and the known intention of its framers.

The partisans of Nullification in the South maintain, on the contrary, that in uniting, the Americans did not intend to reduce themselves to the condition of one and the same people; that they meant to constitute a league of independent States; and that each State consequently keeps its entire sovereignty, if not de facto, at least de jure, and has the right to put its own construction on the laws of Congress and to suspend their execution within its own territory if they are held to be unconstitutional and unjust.

The entire doctrine of Nullification is contained in a sentence spoken by Vice-President Calhoun, the head of that party in the South, before the Senate of the United States in 1833: “The Constitution is a compact to which the States were parties in their sovereign capacity; now, whenever a compact is entered into by parties which acknowledge no tribunal above their authority to decide in the last resort, each of them has a right to judge for itself in relation to the nature, extent, and obligations of the instrument.” It is evident that such a doctrine destroys the very basis of the Federal Constitution and brings back all the evils of the old confederation, from which the Americans were supposed to have been safely delivered.

When South Carolina saw that Congress turned a deaf ear to its remonstrances, it threatened to apply the doctrine of nullification to the federal tariff bill. Congress held to its former system, and at length the storm broke. In the course of 1832 the citizens of South Carolina *b named a national Convention to consult on the extraordinary measures they were called upon to take. On November 24th of the same year this Convention promulgated a law, in the form of a decree, that annulled the federal tariff law, forbade the collection of the duties the law commands, and refused to recognize any appeal to the federal courts. *c This decree was to take effect only in the following February, and it was intimated that if Congress changed the tariff before then, South Carolina might be induced to go no further with her threats; a vague wish was afterwards expressed to submit the question to an extraordinary assembly of all the confederate States.

b [ That is to say, the majority of the people, for the opposing party, called the Union party, always formed a very strong and active minority. Carolina may have about 47,000 electors; 30,000 were in favor of nullification and 17,000 opposed to it.]

c [ This decree was preceded by a report of the committee that drafted it, explaining the motives and object of the law. The following passage occurs in it, p. 34: — “When the rights reserved by the Constitution to the different States are deliberately violated, it is the duty and the right of those States to interfere, in order to check the progress of the evil; to resist usurpation, and to maintain, within their respective limits, those powers and privileges which belong to them as independent sovereign States. If they were destitute of this right, they would not be sovereign. South Carolina declares that she acknowledges no tribunal upon earth above her authority. She has indeed entered into a solemn compact of union with the other States; but she demands, and will exercise, the right of putting her own construction upon it; and when this compact is violated by her sister States, and by the Government which they have created, she is determined to avail herself of the unquestionable right of judging what is the extent of the infraction, and what are the measures best fitted to obtain justice.”]

In the meantime South Carolina armed her militia and prepared for war. But Congress, which had slighted its suppliant subjects, listened to their complaints as soon as they were found to have taken up arms. *d A law was passed under which the tariff duties were to be reduced progressively over ten years, until they were brought so low as not to exceed the amount of revenue the government needed. *e Thus Congress completely abandoned the principle of the tariff and substituted a mere fiscal impost for a system of protective duties. *f The government of the Union, to conceal its defeat, resorted to an expedient very much in vogue with feeble governments. It yielded the point de facto but remained inflexible on the principles in question; and while Congress was altering the tariff law, it passed another bill giving the President extraordinary powers, enabling him to overcome by force a resistance that was by then no longer to be feared.
